data: © Soviet Academy of Sciences (historical). Lander deployed Lunokhod 2 in Le Monnier crater. Lunokhod 2 traversed ~39 km — record until Opportunity (2014).
Luna 21 lander + Lunokhod 2 rover (final resting position)

Lunokhod 2 was the second of two Soviet lunar rovers (1973). Driven by a 5-person ground crew rotating in shifts at the IKI control centre. In 4 months it covered ~39 km — the lunar-surface distance record that stood for 41 years until NASA's Opportunity Mars rover passed it in 2014. Carried French laser retroreflectors that are still used for Earth-Moon ranging today.
Long-distance teleoperated mobility — proved a remote crew can drive an unmanned vehicle across an alien surface in real time (with light-delay).

Luna 21 landed in Le Monnier Crater on January 15, 1973 — and deployed Lunokhod 2, the successor to the world's first lunar rover. Lunokhod 2 drove 42.1 km over 4 months — a record that stood until NASA's Opportunity surpassed it on Mars in July 2014, 41 years later. Returned 80,000 TV images and 86 panoramic sweeps before a regolith pile fell onto the radiator and overheated the rover.
Lunokhod 2 — driving the lunar terra record (42 km)
Lunokhod 2 — improved over Lunokhod 1: more cameras, finer steering control, third-axis manipulator, larger solar panels.
Lunokhod 2 chassis being prepared for shipment — eight independent wheel motors, each with its own torque-feedback control loop.
Lunokhod 2 photographed by its panoramic camera — long shadow stretching across the lunar surface.
42.1 km traverse map — the rover crossed mare basalt, climbed crater walls, and inspected dozens of rocks across four lunar days.
Final position imaged by LRO in 2010 — Lunokhod 2 came to rest after regolith from a steep crater wall buried its radiator panel.
Orrery reference map of LROC imagery and the Lunokhod 2 traverse data

Illustrated block map of the Luna 21 landing site in Le Monnier crater: the Luna 21 lander stands on the plain, and the route of Lunokhod 2 leads to the foot of a ridge and on to the rover’s last position, near the Fossa Recta rille.
